review.summary: Reviewed the CLI client for concurrency, panics and unwraps. One demonstrated remote-triggerable panic: the download status-line error path slices a remote-controlled String at a fixed byte offset, which panics on a non-ASCII boundary. Two lower-severity items: blocking stdout writes under a std mutex inside async tasks, and panics on huge user-supplied durations. Most other unwraps and expects are on local, bounded, or non-poisoning paths.

findings.title: Download status error path slices remote text at a fixed byte offset and can panic
findings.prerequisites: The client runs download() (probe --bulk does not download, but bench and soak do) against a malicious listen node that replies with a status line that does not start with 'ok bytes=' and is not a 'refused' reply. read_status_line returns up to about 256 bytes or more if no newline appears, so the status can be longer than 100 bytes. Byte 100 must fall inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character, which the attacker controls (for example 99 ASCII bytes followed by a 2-byte character).
findings.impact: Panic in the client task that aborts the whole CLI command (tokio::main unwinds to process exit 101). A malicious listener can crash probe, bench or soak at will. The error path is reached only when the announced size is wrong, so it is a demonstrated code defect reachable from remote bytes, not a hypothetical.
findings.evidence: let announced: u64 = status.strip_prefix("ok bytes=").and_then(|n| n.trim().parse().ok()).with_context(|| { format!("listener does not support downloads (an older golem-p2p?): {}", &status[..status.len().min(100)]) })?; with status built by String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf) in read_status_line, which allows buf.len() > 256 before breaking.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate on a char boundary, for example with status.chars().take(100).collect::<String>() or by truncating the bytes before from_utf8_lossy. Add a unit test with a multi-byte character straddling byte 100.
findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code defect by reading. Confirm with a unit test that calls the status parsing with a 100-byte-straddling UTF-8 string, or with a fake listener that sends such a line.

findings.title: Blocking stdout write while holding a std mutex inside async tasks
findings.prerequisites: The stdout consumer of --json output stops reading (pipe full, controller hung). Events are emitted from async tasks (observer tasks, pinger, telemetry) on tokio worker threads.
findings.impact: Each emit blocks a runtime worker thread inside writeln! while the sealed std::sync::Mutex is held, so other emitters block on the lock as well. Enough stalled workers can freeze connection handling and the request path. This is a hypothesis that needs a test with a non-reading stdout pipe; it is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence: fn write(&self, line: &str, last: bool) { let mut sealed = self.inner.sealed.lock().expect("poisoned"); if *sealed { return; } let mut stdout = std::io::stdout().lock(); let _ = writeln!(stdout, "{line}"); let _ = stdout.flush(); *sealed = last; }
findings.suggested_fix: Send events over a bounded channel to one dedicated writer thread, or use spawn_blocking for the write, and drop or count events when the channel is full instead of blocking the caller.
findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis: run a probe --json with stdout piped to a process that stops reading, and check whether the runtime stalls. The sealed lock also needs a check for lock poisoning, which is unlikely since nothing panics while holding it.

findings.title: Huge user-supplied durations overflow Instant arithmetic and panic
findings.prerequisites: The operator passes a very large --duration or --timeout (parse::duration accepts any value that Duration::try_from_secs_f64 accepts, up to about 1.8e19 seconds). This is local operator input, not remote input.
findings.impact: tokio Instant addition panics on overflow, so probe aborts at startup with a panic instead of a clean argument error. Exit code and message are unhelpful, but the impact is limited to the local operator. The same pattern appears in end + timeout on line 193 and in upload() start + t, which are not reached remotely.
findings.evidence: let end = tokio::time::Instant::now() + duration; // A request in flight at the end may take up to one more timeout. let hard_end = end + timeout;
findings.suggested_fix: Use checked_add in parse::duration or at the call sites, and return a clap error when the deadline cannot be represented; cap the accepted range to something like a few days.
findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated by arithmetic reasoning: run probe with --duration 18446744073709551615 and confirm the panic. Low practical risk, since the input comes from the operator.

limitations: bench.rs, soak.rs, listen.rs, telemetry, registry and record.rs were not supplied. Their unwraps, Duration arithmetic and task joins could not be checked, and the listener side of the wire protocol (what a malicious listen node can send) is inferred only from the client code.

The Endpoint internals in golem_p2p endpoint.rs (request timeouts, connection handling, Connection::paths and home_relay_status) were not supplied, so whether requests without an explicit timeout can hang, and whether the watch channels can stall, is unknown.

The clippy lint locations (expect on sealed/first_direct locks, cast_possible_truncation, arithmetic_side_effects in out.rs and probe.rs) were checked by reading. The main cases do not show reachable panics: the locks hold no code that can panic, the casts are on bounded values, and the Stats sum is over locally measured durations.
No runtime testing was done, so the medium-confidence concurrency finding is a hypothesis.
